blocks.text: Two triangles with angles 40°, 60°, 80°; the first has its 40°-side of length 6, the second 9, a ratio of 3:2. If the first has area 20, the second has area `20 x (3/2)^2 = 45`, not 30.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: Match corresponding sides by the angles they sit opposite, not by the order they are written in.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: Its sides are always in the ratio `1 : sqrt(3) : 2`. The shortest side (`x`) faces the 30° angle, the hypotenuse (`2x`) faces the 90°, and the middle side (`x sqrt(3)`) faces the 60°. It is exactly half of an equilateral triangle cut down the middle.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A 30-60-90 triangle with hypotenuse 10 has a short side of 5 and a long leg of `5sqrt(3) ≈ 8.66`. This also gives the height of an equilateral triangle of side 10: `5sqrt(3)`.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: Match sides to angles, not to position in the picture. Given the *long leg* as 6, the short side is `6/sqrt(3) = 2sqrt(3)`, not 3.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: An isosceles right triangle: two equal legs and a hypotenuse `sqrt(2)` times as long, ratio `1 : 1 : sqrt(2)`. It is a square cut along its diagonal, which is why the diagonal of a square with side `s` is `s sqrt(2)`.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Legs of 5 give a hypotenuse of `5sqrt(2) ≈ 7.07`. Backwards: a hypotenuse of 10 gives legs of `10/sqrt(2) = 5sqrt(2) ≈ 7.07`. So a square with diagonal 10 has side `5sqrt(2)` and area 50.

items.label: Splitting a triangle into special right triangles

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: When a triangle has awkward angles, drop a perpendicular from a vertex to the opposite side and look for the two special triangles inside it. An angle of 105° splits into 45 + 60, and 75° into 45 + 30 — and suddenly the whole figure is computable with known ratios.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A triangle with angles 30°, 105°, 45° and one known side. Drop the height from the 105° vertex: it splits into a 30-60-90 and a 45-45-90 sharing that height. Find the height from the known side, use each ratio to get the two base pieces, and add the two areas.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: The perpendicular must land inside the triangle for the areas to add. For an obtuse triangle it may fall outside, in which case you subtract instead.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
Four sets of whole numbers satisfy `a^2 + b^2 = c^2` often enough to be worth knowing by sight: **3-4-5**, **5-12-13**, **8-15-17** and **7-24-25**. Every multiple of a triple is also a triple, so 6-8-10 and 9-12-15 come free.

Recognising one saves you a square-root calculation, and recognising a *near*-miss saves you from assuming a right angle that is not there.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A right triangle with legs 8 and 15 has hypotenuse 17 — no calculation needed. Legs of 9 and 12 give 15, since that is `3 x (3-4-5)`. And if a triangle has sides 5, 12 and 14, it is *not* right-angled, however familiar the 5 and 12 look.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: The largest number must be the hypotenuse. Sides 3, 4 and 5 make a right triangle; sides 3, 5 and a hypotenuse of 4 are impossible.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
For side length `s`, the area is

`area = (sqrt(3) x s^2)/4`

It follows from the 30-60-90 ratios: the height of an equilateral triangle is `s sqrt(3)/2`, and area is half base times height.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: An equilateral triangle of side 6 has area `(sqrt(3) x 36)/4 = 9sqrt(3) ≈ 15.6`. Doubling the side to 12 quadruples the area to `36sqrt(3)`, because area depends on `s^2`.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: `area = base x height`, where the height is the **perpendicular** distance between the two parallel sides — not the length of the slanted side. A parallelogram is a rectangle that has been pushed over, and pushing it over does not change base or height.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A parallelogram with base 10 and slant side 6 leaning at 30° has height `6 x sin(30°) = 3`, so its area is 30, not 60. If the question gives you the height directly as 4, the area is simply 40.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: Using the slanted side as the height is the classic error, and it always overestimates.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: `area = ((base1 + base2)/2) x height`: the average of the two parallel sides times the perpendicular distance between them. You are really finding the width of the "average" rectangle.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A trapezoid with parallel sides 8 and 12 and height 5 has area `((8 + 12)/2) x 5 = 10 x 5 = 50`. If the two bases were equal it would be a parallelogram, and the formula would collapse to base times height.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
With `n` sides of length `s` and apothem `a` (the perpendicular distance from the centre to the middle of a side):

`area = (n x s x a)/2`

The polygon splits into `n` identical triangles, each with base `s` and height `a`. Since `n x s` is the perimeter, this is also "half perimeter times apothem".

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A regular hexagon of side 6 has apothem `3sqrt(3) ≈ 5.196`, so its area is `(6 x 6 x 5.196)/2 ≈ 93.5`. Cross-check with six equilateral triangles of side 6: `6 x 9sqrt(3) = 54sqrt(3) ≈ 93.5` ✓.

items.label: For a fixed perimeter, regular is biggest

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
Among all shapes with the same perimeter and the same number of sides, the regular one encloses the most area, and the further from regular the shape gets, the smaller its area. Pushing a square into a long thin rectangle keeps the perimeter but loses area fast.

Across different numbers of sides the same logic continues: more sides means more area for the same perimeter, with the circle as the winner.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Perimeter 40: a 10 x 10 square gives area 100; a 15 x 5 rectangle gives 75; a 19 x 1 rectangle gives 19. A circle with circumference 40 has radius `40/(2pi) ≈ 6.37` and area ≈ 127, beating every polygon.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: This is about a *fixed perimeter*. Two shapes with the same area can have wildly different perimeters, and the comparison reverses.

items.label: A regular hexagon inscribed in a circle

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
For a regular hexagon inscribed in a circle, the side equals the radius: `s = r`. The hexagon splits into six equilateral triangles meeting at the centre, each with all sides equal to the radius.

The pattern around it is worth knowing: with fewer sides the side is longer than the radius (a square gives `s = r sqrt(2)`), and with more sides the side is shorter.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A regular hexagon inscribed in a circle of radius 6 has sides of 6, perimeter 36, and area `6 x (sqrt(3) x 36/4) = 54sqrt(3) ≈ 93.5`. The circle's area is `36pi ≈ 113`, so the hexagon fills about 83% of it.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
`volume = pi r^2 h` — the circular base area times the height.

`surface area = 2 pi r^2 + 2 pi r h` — the two circular ends plus the curved side, which unrolls into a rectangle of height `h` and width equal to the circumference `2 pi r`.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A cylinder with radius 3 and height 10: volume `= pi x 9 x 10 = 90pi ≈ 283`. Surface area `= 2pi(9) + 2pi(3)(10) = 18pi + 60pi = 78pi ≈ 245`.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: Doubling the radius quadruples the volume but doubling the height only doubles it — radius appears squared, so questions that change the radius have outsized effects.

items.label: For a fixed volume, regular means less surface area

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: The three-dimensional partner of the perimeter rule: for a given volume, the more regular (more compact) the solid, the smaller its surface area. Stretch a solid into a long thin shape and the surface area climbs while the volume stays put. The sphere is the extreme winner; among boxes, the cube is.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Volume 64: a 4 x 4 x 4 cube has surface area 96. A 16 x 2 x 2 box has the same volume but surface area `2(32 + 32 + 4) = 136`. A sphere of volume 64 has surface area about 77.

items.label: The longest diagonal of a shape

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: The longest diagonal joins the two furthest-apart points, which in a box means travelling across the width, the depth **and** the height at once — a corner to its diametrically opposite corner. It is the answer to "what is the longest rod that fits inside".

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In a rectangular room, the longest straight line is not along the floor but from one bottom corner up to the opposite top corner. A face diagonal of a 3 x 4 x 12 box is only 5, while the true longest diagonal is 13.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
`diagonal = sqrt(length^2 + width^2 + depth^2)`

It is Pythagoras applied twice: once across the base to get the floor diagonal, then again vertically using that diagonal and the height.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A 3 x 4 x 12 box: `sqrt(9 + 16 + 144) = sqrt(169) = 13`. For a cube of side `s` the formula collapses to `s sqrt(3)`, so a cube of side 5 has longest diagonal `5sqrt(3) ≈ 8.66`.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: If the small box's dimensions divide exactly into the big box's, you may simply divide the volumes. If they do **not** divide exactly, that shortcut overcounts, because the leftover slivers cannot be reassembled. Instead work out how many fit along each dimension, round each down, and multiply.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: How many 2 x 2 x 2 cubes fit in a 10 x 10 x 10 box? Everything divides evenly: `1000/8 = 125`, and `5 x 5 x 5 = 125` agrees. Now try 3 x 3 x 3 cubes in the same box: volume division suggests `1000/27 ≈ 37`, but per dimension you fit only `10/3 → 3`, so the true answer is `3 x 3 x 3 = 27`.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: You may also be allowed to rotate the small box. If the dimensions differ, test the orientations — one of them often fits noticeably more.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
Mixing two solutions is a weighted average: the concentration of the result sits between the two originals, pulled toward whichever contributes more volume.

If mixture A is `a%` strong with volume `x`, and mixture B is `b%` strong with volume `y`, the final concentration is

`(ax + by)/(x + y)`

The numerator is the total amount of the important substance; the denominator is the total volume.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: 30 litres of 20% acid mixed with 10 litres of 60% acid: `(0.20 x 30 + 0.60 x 10)/40 = (6 + 6)/40 = 12/40 = 30%`. Note the answer is much closer to 20% than to 60%, because there is three times as much of the weak solution.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: The result must always lie strictly between the two concentrations. If your answer falls outside that range, you have made an arithmetic slip.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
When you know the target concentration and need the **ratio** of the two mixtures, you do not need algebra. Take the distance from each starting concentration to the target, and swap them:

`volume of A : volume of B = |z - b| : |z - a|`

where `z` is the target. The mixture further from the target contributes less, so its distance becomes the *other* one's share.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Mix 20% acid with 60% acid to get 30%. Distances: from 20 to 30 is 10, from 60 to 30 is 30. Swapping gives `A : B = 30 : 10 = 3 : 1`. Check with the weighted average: `(0.2 x 3 + 0.6 x 1)/4 = 1.2/4 = 30%` ✓.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: Take care which distance goes with which mixture. The one nearer the target must get the larger share — sanity-check your ratio against that.

items.label: Median of an evenly spaced list

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
For any evenly spaced list, the median equals the mean, and both equal the midpoint of the first and last terms:

`median = (first + last)/2`

You never have to count to the middle. This works for consecutive integers, consecutive multiples, or any arithmetic sequence.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Median of the multiples of 7 between 50 and 200: the first is 56 and the last is 196, so the median is `(56 + 196)/2 = 126`. Median of the integers 1 to 100: `(1 + 100)/2 = 50.5`.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: This holds only when the spacing is even. For an arbitrary list you must sort it and find the middle value (or average the two middle values when the count is even).

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
Quartiles cut an ordered list into four parts: Q1 has a quarter of the data below it, Q2 is the median, Q3 has three quarters below it. The point that trips people up is that the quartile *values* are boundary markers, not members of the quarters — a value sitting exactly on Q1 is not counted inside the first or the second quarter.

The same logic applies to deciles and percentiles: they are dividing lines, and a data point equal to the line belongs to neither side.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For the list 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 the median Q2 is 4.5 with four values each side; Q1 is 2.5 and Q3 is 6.5. So "how many values are in the third quarter" means those strictly between Q2 and Q3, namely 5 and 6.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: Different textbooks compute quartiles slightly differently. On the GRE the interquartile range `Q3 - Q1` is what usually matters, and it is robust to those differences.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
Variance measures how spread out a list is. Take each term's distance from the mean, square it so that positives and negatives do not cancel, add those up, and divide by how many terms there are.

`variance = sum of (term - mean)^2 / N`

Squaring is what makes outliers count heavily: a term twice as far from the mean contributes four times as much.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For 2, 4, 6 the mean is 4. Differences are -2, 0, 2; squares are 4, 0, 4; the total is 8; divide by 3 to get a variance of `8/3 ≈ 2.67`.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
Standard deviation is the square root of the variance, which brings the measure back into the same units as the data. The procedure:

1. Find the mean.
2. Subtract the mean from each term.
3. Square each difference.
4. Add the squares.
5. Divide by `N`.
6. Take the square root.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For 2, 4, 6: mean 4; differences -2, 0, 2; squares 4, 0, 4; sum 8; divide by 3 → 2.67; square root → **1.63**. For 1, 4, 7 the same procedure gives `sqrt(6) ≈ 2.45` — the same mean but more spread, hence a larger SD.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: Most GRE questions only need you to *compare* standard deviations, which you can often do by eye: the list whose values sit further from the mean has the larger SD, regardless of the arithmetic.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: The two differ only in the divisor. Population SD divides by `N`; sample SD divides by `N - 1`. Dividing by a smaller number makes the sample SD slightly larger, which compensates for a sample tending to understate the spread of the population it came from.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: For 2, 4, 6 the population SD is `sqrt(8/3) ≈ 1.63` and the sample SD is `sqrt(8/2) = 2`. The GRE means population SD unless it explicitly says "sample".

items.label: What transformations do to standard deviation

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
Apply the same change to every term in a list and the spread reacts predictably. **Adding or subtracting** a constant shifts everything together and leaves the standard deviation unchanged. **Multiplying or dividing** by a constant scales the SD by that same factor (by its absolute value, since SD is never negative).

The mean, by contrast, changes under both operations.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The list 2, 4, 6 has SD ≈ 1.63. Add 100 to each term to get 102, 104, 106: the SD is still 1.63, though the mean jumps from 4 to 104. Multiply the original by 3 to get 6, 12, 18: the SD triples to ≈ 4.90.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: Variance scales by the *square* of the factor, so multiplying by 3 multiplies the variance by 9 while multiplying the SD by 3.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
Standardizing rewrites each value as the number of standard deviations it sits from the mean — its z-score. Two steps: subtract the mean from every value, then divide each result by the standard deviation. The new list always has mean 0 and standard deviation 1.

`z = (value - mean)/SD`

This is what lets you compare positions across different scales.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: The list 2, 8 has mean 5 and population SD 3. Standardized it becomes `(2-5)/3 = -1` and `(8-5)/3 = 1`, i.e. -1 and 1. So a score of 8 is "one standard deviation above the mean".

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
The bell curve is symmetric about the mean, and the GRE expects you to know how the area splits. Within 1 SD of the mean lies about **68%** of the data (34% each side). The band between 1 and 2 SDs holds about **28%** (14% each side). Beyond 2 SDs lies about **4%** (2% each side).

Cumulatively: about 68% within one SD, about 96% within two. Each half of the curve holds 50%, so `34 + 14 + 2 = 50` on each side — a useful check when you are reconstructing the picture.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Test scores are normally distributed with mean 500 and SD 100. Between 400 and 600 lie 68% of scores. Above 700 (two SDs up) lie 2%. Between 600 and 700 lie 14%. And a score of 700 is at roughly the 98th percentile, since `50 + 34 + 14 = 98`.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: Practise drawing the curve with 2 / 14 / 34 / 34 / 14 / 2 written under the sections. Almost every normal-distribution question is answered by reading numbers off that sketch.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
A **set** is an unordered collection with no duplicates, written in braces `{2, 5, 9}`, and it may be infinite. Its size is written `|S|`. A **list** is ordered, may repeat values, and is always finite.

The distinction decides which counting tool applies: questions about sets lead to combinations and inclusion–exclusion, questions about lists lead to permutations.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: `{1, 2, 3}` and `{3, 2, 1}` are the same set; the lists (1, 2, 3) and (3, 2, 1) are different. `{1, 1, 2}` is really just `{1, 2}` with two elements, whereas the list (1, 1, 2) genuinely has three entries.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
Add the two group sizes and subtract the overlap, which you have otherwise counted twice:

`|A or B| = |A| + |B| - |A and B|`

Rearranged, it also finds the overlap when you know the total, which is the more common exam form.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: In a class of 30, 18 take French and 15 take Spanish, and everyone takes at least one. How many take both? `30 = 18 + 15 - both`, so `both = 3`. If instead 4 students took neither, the equation becomes `30 - 4 = 18 + 15 - both`, giving 7.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: Read carefully whether the total includes people in *neither* group. Those have to be removed before the formula applies.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
With three groups the formula extends by adding back the triple overlap, which the pairwise subtractions removed once too often:

`|A or B or C| = |A| + |B| + |C| - |A and B| - |B and C| - |A and C| + |A and B and C|`

There is a second version, used when a question tells you how many are in **exactly** two groups rather than at least two:

`total = |A| + |B| + |C| - (exactly two) - 2 x (all three)`

Which one you need depends entirely on the wording, so identify that first.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: 40 students, 20 play football, 18 basketball, 16 tennis, 8 play football and basketball, 6 basketball and tennis, 5 football and tennis, and 3 play all three. Then `20+18+16-8-6-5+3 = 38` play at least one, so 2 play none.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: "8 play football and basketball" normally means *at least* those two, including anyone who also plays tennis. If the question says "only football and basketball", use the second formula.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: If one choice has `a` options and an independent second choice has `b` options, the pair has `a x b` possible outcomes. Extend it to as many stages as you like by multiplying them all together — this is the backbone of every counting question.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: A menu with 4 starters and 3 mains offers `4 x 3 = 12` two-course meals. Add 2 desserts and it becomes `4 x 3 x 2 = 24`. Likewise a 4-digit PIN using digits 0-9 with repeats allowed has `10^4 = 10,000` possibilities.

items.label: AND means multiply, OR means add

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
Decide whether the stages happen **together** or **instead** of each other. If both must happen (this *and* that), multiply. If exactly one happens (this *or* that, but not both), add the possibilities.

Most complex counting questions are a tree of these two operations, so label each branch before computing.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Travel from A to B by 3 roads then B to C by 4 roads: both legs are needed, so `3 x 4 = 12` routes. But if you can travel to C by one of 3 roads **or** by one of 4 different roads, that is `3 + 4 = 7` routes.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: If "or" allows both to happen, adding double-counts the overlap — go back to inclusion–exclusion.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
Something that may be taken or left is a two-way choice: in or out. Give every optional item a factor of 2 and multiply as usual. For `n` optional extras that is `2^n` combinations, including the case where you take none.

To enforce "at least one", count everything and subtract the single case where nothing was chosen.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: 4 ice-cream flavours and 4 optional toppings: `4 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 64` combinations. If at least one topping is compulsory, remove the 4 no-topping cases: `64 - 4 = 60`.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: This "count all, subtract the bad case" move is the standard answer to any "at least one" question, and it is almost always faster than counting the good cases directly.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
When order does **not** matter, the number of ways to choose `r` items from `n` is

`nCr = n!/(r!(n - r)!)`

The `r!` on the bottom divides out all the orderings of the same chosen group, which is exactly what "order does not matter" means.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: How many 3-person committees from 10 people? `10C3 = 10!/(3!7!) = (10 x 9 x 8)/(3 x 2 x 1) = 120`. Note the useful symmetry `nCr = nC(n-r)`: choosing 3 to include is the same as choosing 7 to exclude.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: The giveaway word is "committee", "group", "handshake" or "selection" — anything where swapping two members changes nothing.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
When order **does** matter, the count is

`nPr = n!/(n - r)!`

It is the combination count times `r!`, since each chosen group can be arranged in `r!` ways.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: How many ways to award gold, silver and bronze among 10 runners? `10P3 = 10!/7! = 10 x 9 x 8 = 720`, six times the 120 committees above — because each group of three can be arranged on the podium in `3! = 6` ways.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: Words like "ranking", "order", "podium", "president and treasurer" or "password" signal permutations.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: Rather than recall the formula, draw a blank for each position and fill in how many options it has, then multiply. Each item used up reduces the choices for the next slot by one.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: How many ways to arrange the letters of ABCDE? Five slots: `5 x 4 x 3 x 2 x 1 = 120`, which matches `5P5 = 5!/0! = 120`. Choosing only the first three letters: `5 x 4 x 3 = 60 = 5P3`.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
Handle the restricted positions first, then fill in the rest with the slot method. If a restriction splits into separate scenarios, count each scenario fully and **add** them; if the restrictions apply simultaneously, **multiply** the stage counts.

Two standard tricks: to keep items together, glue them into one block and arrange the blocks (then multiply by the arrangements inside the block); to keep items apart, count everything and subtract the arrangements where they are together.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: How many 4-digit numbers can be made from 1-7 with no repeats if the number must be even? The last slot must be 2, 4 or 6 → 3 options; the remaining three slots take any of the leftover 6 digits: `6 x 5 x 4 = 120`. Total `3 x 120 = 360`.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
Arranging `n` items where some are identical gives fewer distinct results than `n!`, because swapping two identical items changes nothing. Divide by the factorial of each repeat count:

`arrangements = n!/(a! b! ...)`

where `a`, `b`, … are how many times each repeated item appears.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: How many arrangements of the letters in BANANA? `n = 6`, with three As and two Ns, so `6!/(3! 2!) = 720/12 = 60`. For a word with no repeats, like ABCDEF, the division disappears and you get the full `6! = 720`.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: Divide by the factorial of each repeat *separately*; do not add the repeat counts together first. Three As and two Ns means `3! x 2! = 12`, not `5! = 120`.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: Combine the two ideas: split the problem into the sections the restriction creates, count each with the repeats formula, then multiply the sections together (or add, if they are alternative scenarios).

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: How many arrangements of TEXTBOOK have all vowels first and all consonants last? The vowels are E, O, O → `3!/2! = 3` arrangements. The consonants are T, X, T, B, K → `5!/2! = 60`. The two blocks are both required, so multiply: `3 x 60 = 180`.

items.label: Turning a word problem into a counting problem

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
Most counting questions are one of the standard types wearing a disguise. Before calculating, answer three questions: how many items are there, how many are being chosen or arranged, and does order matter? Add a fourth if needed: are repeats allowed?

Order matters → permutation. Order does not → combination. Repeats allowed → plain multiplication (`n^r`). Identical items in a fixed arrangement → divide by the repeat factorials.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: "How many ways can 5 books be placed on a shelf if 2 are identical?" Items: 5, all being arranged, order matters, with one repeat of 2 → `5!/2! = 60`. "How many 3-topping pizzas from 8 toppings?" Choosing 3 of 8, order irrelevant, no repeats → `8C3 = 56`.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
Seating `n` people around a circle gives `(n - 1)!` arrangements rather than `n!`. A circle has no fixed starting point, so rotating everyone by one seat produces the same arrangement — which means each distinct seating has been counted `n` times, and `n!/n = (n - 1)!`.

The practical method: fix one person in place, then arrange the remaining `n - 1` around them.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: 5 people in a row: `5! = 120`. The same 5 around a round table: `4! = 24`. If the seats are numbered — or if the arrangement can be flipped over, as with a bracelet — the count changes again, so read the question carefully.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
For a fixed `n`, the number of combinations peaks when `r` is half of `n`. Choosing about half the items gives the most possible groups, and the counts fall away symmetrically toward `r = 0` and `r = n`, which each have exactly one.

If `n` is odd there is no exact half, so two neighbouring values of `r` tie for the maximum.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: With `n = 6`, the counts run 1, 6, 15, 20, 15, 6, 1 — the maximum is 20 at `r = 3`. With `n = 7` they run 1, 7, 21, 35, 35, 21, 7, 1, so `r = 3` and `r = 4` tie at 35.

items.label: Probability that both A and B happen

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
For **independent** events — where one happening does not change the odds of the other — multiply:

`P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B)`

If the events are not independent, use the conditional version `P(A) x P(B given A)`.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Two fair coin flips both landing heads: `1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4`. But drawing two aces from a deck *without replacement* is not independent: `4/52 x 3/51 = 1/221`, not `(4/52)^2`.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: "Without replacement" is the flag for dependence. The second probability must account for what the first draw removed.

items.label: Probability that A or B happens

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: `P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B)`. It is inclusion–exclusion again: adding the two probabilities double-counts the outcomes where both occur, so subtract that overlap once.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Rolling a die, `P(even) = 3/6` and `P(greater than 3) = 3/6`. The overlap (4 or 6) is `2/6`. So `P(even or greater than 3) = 3/6 + 3/6 - 2/6 = 4/6 = 2/3` — matching the list 2, 4, 5, 6.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
These sound similar and mean opposite things. **Independent** events do not affect each other's chances, so `P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B)`. **Mutually exclusive** events cannot both happen, so `P(A and B) = 0` and `P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B)`.

A consequence worth remembering: for mutually exclusive events `P(A) + P(B) <= 1`, because probabilities summing past 1 would force an overlap.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Two coin flips are independent (both can be heads). Drawing one card that is both a king and a queen is mutually exclusive. Note that two events with non-zero probability cannot be both independent and mutually exclusive — if they cannot co-occur, knowing one happened tells you a great deal about the other.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text: `P(A | B) = P(A and B)/P(B)` — the chance of A *given that* B has happened. Conditioning on B shrinks the world to just the outcomes where B occurred, so you re-scale by dividing by `P(B)`.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Roll a die; what is the probability it is a 2 given that it is even? `P(2 and even) = 1/6`, `P(even) = 1/2`, so `P(2 | even) = (1/6)/(1/2) = 1/3`. That matches intuition: among 2, 4, 6, one of the three is a 2.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: `P(A | B)` and `P(B | A)` are different numbers. The probability of being even given a roll of 2 is 1, not 1/3.

blocks.label: Explanation
blocks.text:
Questions asking for the probability of "at least one" are almost always faster backwards: compute the probability that it never happens and subtract from 1.

`P(at least one) = 1 - P(none)`

Counting the direct way means adding the cases for exactly one, exactly two, exactly three … whereas the complement is a single multiplication.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: Flip a coin 4 times; what is the probability of at least one head? `P(no heads) = (1/2)^4 = 1/16`, so the answer is `15/16`. The direct route would have needed four separate cases.

blocks.label: Watch out
blocks.text: The complement of "at least one" is "none", not "exactly one". Likewise the complement of "at least two" is "zero or one" — both of which you must subtract.
